reviewNotes: No person has reviewed this file.

Story and previous: from IM’s lesson narrative (“less support”; double number lines no longer given), Lesson 12’s and 13’s goals (tape diagrams; 10%, 25%, 50% and 75% as fractions), and IM’s lesson synthesis (the third kind of problem is new today).

Crux is 14.2, as in Premo’s layer. 14.3 (Info Gap, 20 minutes, goal 2) is a fair alternative; its purpose reads as practicing language, and the checker keeps that kind of activity off the crux while another activity brings new math.
CLO: imGoal is IM goal 1, verbatim. Function “explain” and mode “out loud” come from it; the unit’s language progression also names “explain” for Lesson 14, so there is no progression note.

Form: “In my ___, ___ lines up with 100%. ___ is ___ of ___, so ___ is ___% of ___.” It fits both questions: Han (in my table, $15 lines up with 100%; 10% is \(\frac{1}{10}\) of 100%, so $1.50 is 10% of $15) and Clare ($6 is \(\frac{1}{4}\) of $24, so $6 is 25% of $24). It follows IM Lesson 13’s usage, “25% of a quantity is \(\frac14\) of that quantity,” never “25% = \(\frac14\).” “Lines up with” is Premo’s plain word for IM’s “corresponds with.”

Precise terms: “100%,” “% of” (IM’s receptive term for Lesson 14 is “___% of”) and “percentage” (productive in Lesson 15). The board lines can’t hold digits, so the language line says “the whole” for the 100% value.

Numbers checked: 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5; 6 ÷ 24 = 0.25; 60% of 40 = 24; 24 ÷ 25 = 0.96; 24 ÷ 0.4 = 60; 80% of 20 = 16; 6 × 0.8 × 2 = 9.6; 4.5 × 0.6 × 4 = 10.8. Posted sentence: 10 ÷ 50 = 0.2, 20%. Lesson synthesis check: 6 ÷ 30 = 0.2, 20%; it shares no numbers with the cool-down (20 minutes, 80%).
Look-for accepts IM’s two strategies (10% is 2 minutes, then 8 × 2; the table 20 | 100, 2 | 10, 16 | 80) and also \(\frac{8}{10}\) of 20 or a double number line. IM’s answer is 16 minutes.

Per D1: Three Reads to launch, an MLR 8 frame at release, MLR 2 Collect and Display in the synthesis. IM’s crux routine is MLR 7 Compare and Connect; its move is built in (option 3): students say where 15 times \(\frac{1}{10}\) shows in each diagram, then why one double number line can’t solve both questions. Those are IM’s two questions from the support and the synthesis.

14.2 is 10 minutes, the same as 6.3.7’s crux. Card times are estimates: Three Reads about 2 minutes, quiet think time about 3, partner sharing about 2, the comparison from about 8. It is tight; a reviewer should confirm the comparison fits. IM’s launch also displays coupons first, which this plan keeps brief.
14.2 momentIds: m2, m6, m7. m3 (the sale price slip) is a back-pocket line; m5 (Compare and Connect slipping) is covered by the synthesis card’s checks.
14.3 momentIds: m8 (a data card read out) and m10 (40% of $24, Premo’s). Both need momentCriteria here, since neither is rehearsed in Premo’s layer. m9 (25 tick marks) is a back-pocket line.

NEW (Premo-written, unreviewed): the board words for Pairs A, B and C on the synthesis card; the m6 student’s line; all ifNot questions; every goingOn line; the level frames, stretches and nonverbal ways in.
The Info Gap card text comes from IM’s Teacher Guide (printed page 237), copied in tg/6.3.14.json notes. Data Card 1’s line is quoted on the m8 card.
Non-crux activities carry no language supports (D7).
story: Lesson 14 is late in the percentages section. Diagrams are no longer given: students choose a tape diagram, double number line or table, and find a percentage itself for the first time.
previous: In Lessons 12 and 13 students used tape diagrams and benchmark percentages; today they pick their own diagram and also ask what percentage one amount is of another.

clo.imGoal: Choose and create a tape diagram, double number line diagram, or table to solve problems involving percentages and explain (orally) the solution method.
clo.form: In my ___, ___ lines up with 100%. ___ is ___ of ___, so ___ is ___% of ___.

board.content: We will choose a diagram or table to solve percentage problems, starting from the whole amount.
board.language: We will explain, out loud, how our diagram finds the “percentage,” naming “the whole” and using “% of.”

clo.exemplar: In my double number line, $24 lines up with 100%. $6 is \(\frac{1}{4}\) of $24, so $6 is 25% of $24. The percentage off is 25%.
clo.lookFor: The explanation names 20 minutes as 100% and finds 80% of it, 16 minutes: by 10% is 2 minutes, then 8 × 2; by a table (20 | 100, 2 | 10, 16 | 80); or by \(\frac{8}{10}\) of 20 or a double number line.

posted.sentence: In my table, $50 lines up with 100%. $10 is \(\frac{1}{5}\) of $50, so $10 is 20% of $50.

barriers: Holding a partial product in memory without writing it down.
Multiplying by a decimal like 0.8 as “8 tenths of.”
misconceptions: Working left to right only, when regrouping the factors is easier.
backPocket: Did anyone solve the problem in a different way?
Which two factors did you multiply first, and why?
Is your answer more or less than 12? How do you know?
activities.grouping: Whole class: one problem at a time, 1 minute of quiet think time each, a signal when ready.
activities.monitor: Listen for which factors students multiply first. Gather two or three different strategies per problem.

strategies: Tape diagram: $15 in 10 equal parts; one part, 10%, is $1.50. For Clare, $24 in 4 parts of $6, so $6 is 25%.
Double number line: $15 at 100%, ticks every 10% ($1.50 apart). For Clare, $24 at 100%, ticks every 25% ($6 apart).
Table: 15 | 100, then times \(\frac{1}{10}\) to 1.5 | 10. For Clare, 24 | 100, then times \(\frac{1}{4}\) to 6 | 25.
barriers: The two questions ask for different things: dollars saved, then a percentage off.
“Normal price,” “saves” and “percentage off” on a coupon may be unfamiliar words.
misconceptions: Answering Clare’s question with “$6,” the dollars saved, not the percentage.
Finding Han’s sale price, $13.50, instead of what he saves.
Using one double number line for both questions, with the same amount at 100%.
Language: “It’s 25,” with no “%,” no “of,” and no 100% value.
backPocket: What does the question ask you to find?
Is $13.50 what he pays, or what he saves?
What lines up with 100% for Han? For Clare?
How many equal parts make $24? What is each part?
activities.grouping: Alone, then pairs: quiet think time to answer both questions, then each partner explains their reasoning.
activities.monitor: Track who draws a tape diagram, a double number line or a table, to share in that order. Check each student’s 100% value for both questions.

strategies: Card 1: 60% of $40 is $24 (10% is $4, times 6), so Jada can afford only Device A.
Card 1, Device B: $25 is 100%, so each dollar is 4%; $24 is \(24 \boldcdot 4\), 96%. Or $24 is $1 short, so 100% − 4%.
Card 2: $24 is 40%, so $6 is 10% and $60 is 100%. Device D costs $60.
barriers: Asking for one specific fact, and saying why it’s needed, is new talk for many students.
Card 1’s data gives Jada’s money only as a percentage of Device C.
misconceptions: The data-card partner reads out the card or works out $24 for the partner.
Drawing all 25 tick marks for Device B instead of using each dollar as 4%.
Taking 40% of $24 for Device D, treating $24 as the whole.
backPocket: What specific information do you need? Why do you need it?
If $25 is 100%, what is each dollar worth?
Is $24 the whole price, or part of it?
activities.grouping: Pairs: one problem card and one data card; switch roles for the second set.
activities.monitor: Listen for problem-card partners asking for one fact at a time and saying why. Note different strategies for Device B, least to most efficient, to share.

m8: Stopped the read-out and had the pair start again
Had the data partner ask what information was needed
Kept the calculating with the problem-card partner
m10: Asked whether $24 is the whole or a part
Pointed to the 40% on the data card

threeReads.say: Listen as I read. No numbers yet: what is happening?
threeReads.listenFor: Han and Clare go shopping, and each uses a coupon to pay less.

threeReads.say: Read it again. What does each number tell us?
threeReads.listenFor: $15 and $24 are normal prices. 10% is Han’s coupon. $6 is what Clare saves.

threeReads.say: Read it once more. How might we solve each question?
threeReads.listenFor: Draw a tape diagram, double number line or table for each person, with the normal price at 100%.

release.successCriteria: Say what lines up with 100% first. Then name your answer with “% of.”
release.say: Start with what lines up with 100%. Then use “% of.”
talkMoments: After quiet think time, partners take turns explaining one question each with Today’s frame.
When partners compare, each says what lines up with 100% in their diagram for Clare.

emerging.stretch: They say what kind of diagram they used and point to 100% on it.
emerging.nonverbal: They circle the 100% value on their diagram, then circle the pair that answers the question.

developing.frame: ___ lines up with 100%. ___ is ___ of ___, so ___ is ___% of ___.
developing.stretch: They add how they split the whole: into 10 parts, or into 4 parts.
developing.nonverbal: They draw an arrow on their table from the 100% row to the answer row, and write the fraction on it.

expanding.frame: In my ___, ___ lines up with 100%. ___ is ___ of ___, so ___ is ___% of ___.
expanding.stretch: They check the answer a second way, such as a table against a double number line.
expanding.nonverbal: They mark the equal parts on their double number line and tap each one as they count the percent.

steps: During partner talk, scribe students’ words as said, such as “the whole” or “the full price,” and write “100%” beside them.
Call pairs in IM’s order for Han’s question: a tape diagram, then a double number line, then a table. Draw each as they explain.
Scribe each pair’s words beside its diagram; add “% of” or “\(\frac{1}{10}\) of” next to their words, not in place of them.
Ask: “Where do you see 15 times \(\frac{1}{10}\) in each one?” Then: “Could one double number line solve Clare’s question too?” Students make the connections; you scribe them.
Leave the board up for the lesson synthesis and the cool-down.
synthesis.prompt: Could one double number line solve both questions? Why not?
synthesis.sounds: No. Han’s line has $15 at 100%, and Clare’s has $24 at 100%. The whole is different, so we need two lines.

rehearsal.name: Do the warm-up yourself
rehearsal.where: Before class. Solve the number talk: two products, found mentally.
show: \(6\boldcdot (0.8)\boldcdot 2\)
\((4.5)\boldcdot (0.6)\boldcdot 4\)
rehearsal.ask: Find each product in your head. Which factors did you multiply first?
rehearsal.aim: Know both products and two ways to get each.
checks: Got 9.6 and 10.8
Multiplied the whole numbers first in at least one problem
Found a second way for each problem

rehearsal.name: Hold back your own strategy
rehearsal.where: About 4 minutes into Activity 14.1. One student has shared a strategy for the first problem, and you recorded it.
show: On the board: \(6\boldcdot (0.8)\boldcdot 2\)
Recorded: “6 times 2 is 12, then 0.8 of 12 is 9.6.”
rehearsal.ask: You want to show the class your way next. What do you do instead?
rehearsal.aim: A second student shares a different strategy before you show any.
say: Did anyone solve the problem in a different way?
checks: Asked for another student’s way before showing any
Recorded the first strategy as the student said it
Didn’t demonstrate a strategy of your own
rehearsal.why: IM: in a Number Talk, the teacher selects students to share different strategies. Their ways go on the board, not yours.

rehearsal.name: Do the coupon task yourself
rehearsal.where: Before class. Solve the task students do today: two coupon questions, no diagram given.
show: Han buys an item with a normal price of $15, and uses a 10% off coupon. How much does he save by using the coupon?
Clare buys an item with a normal price of $24, but saves $6 by using a coupon. For what percentage off is this coupon?
rehearsal.ask: Answer both questions. Draw a diagram or table for each.
rehearsal.aim: Know both answers and three ways to show each.
notes: Tape diagram: $15 in 10 equal parts, each 10%. For Clare, $24 in 4 equal parts of $6.
Double number line: $15 at 100%, ticks every 10%. For Clare, $24 at 100%, ticks every 25%.
Table: 15 | 100, then times \(\frac{1}{10}\). For Clare, 24 | 100, then times \(\frac{1}{4}\).
IM shares a tape diagram first, then a double number line or a table.
checks: Got $1.50 for Han and 25% for Clare
Put $15 at 100% for Han and $24 at 100% for Clare
Drew two separate diagrams or tables, not one

rehearsal.name: Read the task three times
rehearsal.where: Start of Activity 14.2. You’ve shown a few coupons, some dollars off and some percent off. The task is up.
show: Han and Clare go shopping, and they each have a coupon. Answer each question and show your reasoning.
Han buys an item with a normal price of $15, and uses a 10% off coupon. How much does he save by using the coupon?
Clare buys an item with a normal price of $24, but saves $6 by using a coupon. For what percentage off is this coupon?
rehearsal.ask: Read the task aloud three times. After each read, ask one question. Nobody solves yet.
rehearsal.aim: Students know what each question asks for before anyone solves.

rounds.ask: You’ve read the task once. What do you ask?
rounds.aim: Students say what is happening, with no numbers.

rounds.ask: You’ve read it twice. What do you ask?
rounds.aim: Students say what each number tells us, and whose it is.

rounds.ask: You’ve read it three times. What do you ask?
rounds.aim: Students suggest diagrams or tables to use, without solving.

checks: Read 1: asked what is happening, with no numbers
Read 2: asked what each number tells us
Read 3: asked how we might solve each question, and took ideas without solving
rehearsal.why: IM: Three Reads makes sure students know what they’re being asked to do. Here, it separates Han’s question, dollars saved, from Clare’s, a percentage off.
runIt: Read 1: read the task aloud. Ask what is happening, with no numbers.
Read 2: read it again. Ask what each number tells us.
Read 3: read it once more. Ask how we might solve each question. Take ideas; nobody solves.

rehearsal.name: Send students to work
rehearsal.where: About 2 minutes into Activity 14.2. Three Reads just ended. Next: quiet think time, then partners explain their reasoning.
rehearsal.ask: What do you tell the class to say first when they explain?
rehearsal.aim: Students know to name the 100% value first, then use “% of.”
say: Start with what lines up with 100%. Then use “% of.”
notes: Success criteria: Say what lines up with 100% first. Then name your answer with “% of.”
When partners talk: after quiet think time, partners take turns explaining one question each with Today’s frame.
Then: when partners compare, each says what lines up with 100% in their diagram for Clare.
checks: Named what every explanation starts with: the 100% value
Pointed to Today’s frame on the board
Told them when they’ll explain to a partner
rehearsal.sounds: In my double number line, $24 lines up with 100%. $6 is \(\frac{1}{4}\) of $24, so $6 is 25% of $24. The percentage off is 25%.
rehearsal.why: IM says students must first decide what value goes with 100%. Naming it before work starts makes it the first thing every explanation says.

rehearsal.name: A student answers in dollars
rehearsal.where: About 4 minutes into Activity 14.2. Students are in quiet think time.
show: Clare’s question: “Clare buys an item with a normal price of $24, but saves $6 by using a coupon. For what percentage off is this coupon?”
Their answer: “$6.”
rehearsal.student: A student wrote “$6” for Clare’s question and moved on.
rehearsal.ask: What do you say to this student?
rehearsal.aim: The student rereads the question and says what it asks for.
say: What does the question ask you to find?
checks: Sent them back to reread the question
Asked what kind of answer the question wants
Didn’t tell them it’s a percentage
rehearsal.goingOn: They read the numbers and found what Clare saved, as Han’s question asked. They haven’t yet noticed this question asks for a percentage.
rehearsal.ifNot: Read the last sentence again. What word tells you what to find?

rehearsal.name: Help a student say it in words
rehearsal.where: About 6 minutes into Activity 14.2. Partners are explaining their reasoning to each other.
show: Their double number line for Clare:
value (dollars): 0, 6, 12, 18, 24
rehearsal.student: A student points to the first tick after 0: “It’s 25. Right there.”
rehearsal.ask: What do you say to this student?
rehearsal.aim: The student says what is 100%, then says $6 as a percent of $24.
checks: Asked every level the same question: what is 100%, and what is $6
Gave their level’s frame or nonverbal way in
Didn’t say the sentence for them
rehearsal.ifNot: Put a finger on 100%. Which dollar amount is above it?
rehearsal.sounds: On my double number line, $24 lines up with 100%. $6 is \(\frac{1}{4}\) of $24, so $6 is 25% of $24.
rehearsal.goingOn: They found the right tick and the right number. What 100% stands for, and that 25 is a percent of $24, isn’t in words yet.

rehearsal.name: Choose who shares first
rehearsal.where: About 7 minutes into Activity 14.2. Partners have explained. You’re about to start the discussion.
show: Three papers for Han’s question:
Pair A · tape diagram: $15 in 10 equal parts, one part labeled $1.50.
Pair B · double number line: $0 to $15 above, 0% to 100% below, ticks every 10%.
Pair C · table: 15 | 100, then 1.5 | 10.
rehearsal.ask: Who do you call first? What do you ask them?
rehearsal.aim: Pairs share in IM’s order: tape diagram, double number line, then table.
say: Start us off. What did you draw for Han’s coupon?
checks: Called a tape diagram first
Followed with a double number line or a table
Didn’t start with the quickest way
rehearsal.why: IM gives the order: a tape diagram first, then a double number line or a table. The tape shows the 10 equal parts plainly, so the others can be read against it.

rehearsal.name: Finish on the board
rehearsal.where: About 8 minutes into Activity 14.2. Pairs A, B and C have shown their diagrams for Han. Their words are on the board.
show: On the board:
Pair A · tape diagram: “10 pieces. Each piece is $1.50.”
Pair B · double number line: “$15 is at the end, so it’s 100%. Go back to the first tick.”
Pair C · table: “Divide both by 10.”
rehearsal.ask: Pair C’s words are up. What do you write beside them? What do you ask next?
rehearsal.aim: Students say why Han and Clare need separate diagrams.
notes: Write beside Pair C’s words: “\(\frac{1}{10}\) of 100%” and “10% of $15.”
Then ask, and let students make the connections:
say: Where do you see 15 times \(\frac{1}{10}\) in each one?
Could one double number line solve Clare’s question too? Why not?
checks: Called pairs in IM’s order: tape diagram, double number line, then table
Wrote students’ own words, with “100%” or “% of” beside them
Asked why one line can’t solve both, and let students answer
rehearsal.sounds: No. Han’s line has $15 at 100%, and Clare’s has $24 at 100%. The whole is different, so we need two lines.
rehearsal.why: IM: Collect and Display turns students’ spoken words into a shared reference. Here it holds IM’s point: two diagrams, because the value for 100% differs.
runIt: During partner talk, scribe students’ words as said, such as “the whole.” Write “100%” beside them.
Call pairs in IM’s order: tape diagram, double number line, table. Draw each as they explain.
Scribe each pair’s words beside its diagram; add “% of” next to their words, not in place of them.
Ask where 15 times \(\frac{1}{10}\) shows in each, then whether one line could solve both. Scribe their answers.
Leave the board up for the lesson synthesis and the cool-down.

rehearsal.name: Do the info gap yourself
rehearsal.where: Before class. Solve both problem cards using the facts on the data cards.
show: Problem Card 1: Which of the devices can Jada afford? What percentage of the money needed for Device B does she have?
Data Card 1: Device A costs $15. Device B costs $25. Device C costs $40. Jada has 60% of the money needed to buy Device C.
Problem Card 2: How much does Device D cost?
Data Card 2: Jada has $24. Jada has 40% of the money needed to buy Device D.
rehearsal.ask: Which devices can Jada afford? What percentage of Device B’s price does she have? What does Device D cost?
rehearsal.aim: Know all three answers and which facts each one needs.
notes: Card 1: 10% of $40 is $4, so 60% is six of those. Compare that with each device’s price.
Device B: $25 is 100%, so each dollar is 4%. Or Jada is $1 short, so 4% short.
Card 2: $24 is 40%, so 10% is a quarter of $24. Then multiply by 10 for 100%.
IM: if time is short, the second set of cards can be optional.
checks: Found Jada has $24, 60% of $40, so she can afford only Device A
Found she has 96% of the money for Device B
Found Device D costs $60

rehearsal.name: Stop a partner reading out the card
rehearsal.where: About 3 minutes into Activity 14.3. Pairs have the first cards. You stop beside one pair.
show: Data Card 1: Device A costs $15. Device B costs $25. Device C costs $40. Jada has 60% of the money needed to buy Device C.
rehearsal.student: The data-card partner reads all four lines aloud, then says: “So she has $24.”
rehearsal.ask: What do you say to this pair?
rehearsal.aim: The problem-card partner asks for each fact and says why they need it.
say: Start again. Data-card partner, ask: “What specific information do you need?”
checks: Stopped the read-out and had the pair start again
Had the data partner ask what information was needed
Kept the calculating with the problem-card partner
rehearsal.why: IM: the info gap gives students a reason to ask for the information a problem needs. A card read aloud skips that, and the data partner does the math.

rehearsal.name: A student finds 40% of $24
rehearsal.where: About 14 minutes into Activity 14.3. Partners have switched roles for the second cards.
show: Problem Card 2: How much does Device D cost?
Data Card 2: Jada has $24. Jada has 40% of the money needed to buy Device D.
Their work: “40% of $24 is $9.60.”
rehearsal.ask: What do you say to this student?
rehearsal.aim: The student sees $24 is a part of Device D’s price, not the whole.
say: Is $24 the whole price, or part of it?
checks: Asked whether $24 is the whole or a part
Pointed to the 40% on the data card
Let them place $24 and 40% themselves
rehearsal.goingOn: They can find a percentage of an amount, the kind of problem from earlier lessons. Here the whole is unknown, and $24 is the part.
rehearsal.ifNot: What does the 40% on the data card describe?

ideas: One fact, 20% of 400 liters is 80 liters, answers three questions: find the part, find the whole, or find the percentage.
Every one starts with what lines up with 100%: here, the full 400-liter tank.
To find what percentage 80 is of 400, ask what fraction of 400 is 80. It is \(\frac{1}{5}\), and \(\frac{1}{5}\) of 100% is 20%.
lessonSynthesis.pointTo: Point to the 14.2 board: Han’s diagram with $15 at 100%, Clare’s with $24 at 100%, and the words beside them. If you taught 14.3, point to its tables too.

check.question: A $30 game is on sale, and you save $6. What percentage off is the sale? Say it with Today’s frame.
check.sounds: In my table, $30 lines up with 100%. $6 is \(\frac{1}{5}\) of $30, so $6 is 20% of $30.

beforeClass: For the launch: have a few coupons to display, some dollars off and some percent off.
For Three Reads in 14.2: display the task, and have the frames for your students’ levels ready to post or hand out.
For Collect and Display (MLR 2): clear board space to draw students’ diagrams side by side, and have a marker ready.
For 14.3: copy and cut the Info Gap: Music Devices cards (1 copy for every 4 students), and plan a one-minute demo with a student.

cuts.note: Keep it short: two or three strategies per problem.
IM: if time is short, the second set of cards can be optional. One problem understood well beats two rushed.
IM gives 10 minutes. Keep the coupon display and Three Reads quick. Never cut quiet think time, partners explaining, or the comparison of diagrams.
